book_text: What breaks first. Per-user recall usually fails before the disk fills. At the default ef_search of 40, an HNSW search returns 40 candidates, and the WHERE clause then discards the rows that belong to other users. If 20 users share the table evenly, about 2 of the 40 belong to the user you asked about. With 5,000 users, usually none do. This is an estimate from the README's arithmetic, not a recall guarantee. The fixes are in the filters gotcha below. 1 Concurrent load also competes for CPU and cache, so measure p95 and p99 at the agent count you expect. No universal row cutoff exists.
reason: Independent tenant labels at 5% and 0.02% selectivity; returned counts and recall measured over the same 200 queries. Arithmetic is an expectation, not a guarantee.
suggested_replacement: With ef_search=40, this book measured mean result counts of 2.025 for 20 equal tenants and 0.005 for 5,000 tenants across 200 queries. These are observations for this fixture, not a per-query recall guarantee.
interpretation: Supports the behavior in these controlled cases; this is not a universal performance bound.

book_text: The index scan runs first and the WHERE clause removes rows afterwards, so a per-user query can return fewer rows than LIMIT . book_text: Expiry has one trap. Values up to 2,592,000 seconds (30 days) are lifetimes counted from now. Larger values are read as Unix timestamps, so 31 days in seconds points into 1970 and expires at once. Use the current Unix time plus the lifetime you want, as tested below. An expiry of 0 means no time expiry, but it does not protect against eviction. Eviction reclaims items at the least-recently-used end within slab classes, so monitor per-slab eviction counters instead of assuming every item lasts until its TTL. 1 2

interpretation: Supports the behavior in these controlled cases; this is not a universal performance bound.
